pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Recording data

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Working Scientifically):** the statutory programme requires pupils are taught to use "gathering and recording data to help in answering questions", alongside "observing closely, using simple equipment" and "identifying and classifying". This is the child's first structured capture of what they notice into a usable form.

- **Standards — US (NGSS SEP 8 / SEP 4, grades K–2):** the K–2 progressions include "record information (observations, thoughts, and ideas)" and "record and share observations" and "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-ESS1-1, K-ESS2-1, K-LS1-1]". Recording data into simple tables, tallies and drawings is the K–2 entry point to handling data.

- **Operational details:** Builds on performing simple tests (prerequisite mt_Wa44s-f8Ws). Three moves: (1) record observations/measurements in a simple TABLE or TALLY CHART; (2) use DRAWINGS or labelled diagrams to record what was seen; and (3) explain how the record helps ANSWER the question. The key idea for this age is that recording is not decoration — it captures information so it can be looked back at and used, and memory alone is unreliable. Feeds forward to presenting data in charts/keys and analysing design tests (dependents mt_7IFpDVNsmt, mt_nNYo5A-7Bl).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). A learner who can record observations in a simple table or tally, use a labelled drawing to record what they saw, and say how the record helps answer the question has met the bar. Choosing between graph types comes later (mt_7IFpDVNsmt, mt_rDjtmDogJr).
bestPractices: Give a genuine reason to record — collect so much or over such a time that memory obviously fails (e.g. tally minibeasts found, weather each day for a week) — so pupils feel WHY we write it down.
Model the tally as counting-as-you-go (the fifth stroke crossing the gate) so recording keeps pace with observing rather than being reconstructed afterwards.
Pair a labelled drawing with a table so pupils see two complementary record types — pictures for what it looked like, tables/tallies for how many.
Always close the loop: after recording, return to the question and ask 'what does our record tell us?' — recording exists to answer questions.
Keep headings and categories decided BEFORE collecting so the table is ready to fill, modelling a tiny bit of planning.
keyRepresentations: A simple two-column table (thing observed | count/measurement)
A tally chart with gated fives
A weather/nature 'over time' record strip (one entry per day)
A question → record → 'what it tells us' loop card
commonMisconceptions: Thinking you can just remember it — not seeing why data must be written down as you go.
Recording after the fact from memory rather than in the moment, losing accuracy.
Treating the drawing/table as the end product ('finished!') rather than something to READ to answer the question.
Muddled tallies (miscounting, not gating fives) that can't be read back.
Inventing categories or changing headings mid-collection so the record can't be totalled.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach recording data as an active skill: capture observations in simple tables, tally charts, and labelled drawings while events happen, then READ the record back to answer the original question. The core insight is that recording is not decoration — it captures information so it can be used later, because memory alone is unreliable. Includes a live capture activity, a read-back-and-choose practice set, and a reference scaffold, each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Live tally-and-table capture
feedback: If you try to just watch and remember, the creatures dart off and the count slips away — mark a tally stroke for each one so you keep pace.
If your tally is muddled (fives not gated, strokes miscounted), it can't be read back — count as you go and cross the gate on every fifth stroke.
After recording, return to the question: 'What does our record tell us? Which has the biggest total?'
If you change a heading partway through, the counts may not match up and are hard to total — decide categories before you start.
activities.rationale: Recording is a doing skill: the child must capture observations as events unfold and then read the record back. A scene that produces events in real time is intended to give a felt reason to record live — if the child relies on memory, the count is easily lost — addressing the core misconception that you can 'just remember it'. Pairing a drawing with a table/tally models two of the simple record types named in the objective (tables, tally charts and drawings). A live on-screen tool is one suitable medium; an equivalent real-world collection (tallying minibeasts in the playground, logging weather daily, or rolling toy cars and recording distances) meets the same objective and should be used where practical.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires gathering and recording data to help in answering questions.
NGSS SEP 4 and SEP 8 at grades K-2 include recording information and observations and using observations to describe patterns.
learnerActions: Before collecting, agree the table headings and categories (e.g. one row per minibeast type, or one row per kind of weather with one mark added each day of the week) so the record is ready to fill.

Watch a scene where events keep happening — minibeasts scuttle across a garden, or the weather changes each day for a week — and mark a tally stroke for each thing as it happens, counting as you go (cross the gate on the fifth stroke).
Add a labelled observational drawing of one thing you saw, alongside the counting table, so you have two complementary record types — a picture for what it looked like and a table/tally for how many.
When the question drops in ('which minibeast did we see most?' / 'which kind of weather did we have on the most days?'), read the answer directly off your own totals.
Say out loud how your record helps answer the question.
activities.intendedInsight: Writing it down as it happens is what makes the question answerable later; a record is something you READ to find an answer, not just something you made and finished.

activities.title: Read the record and choose how to record
feedback: If you pick the wrong total, re-count the tally gate by gate — each full gate is five.
For 'which was most', find the row with the biggest count, not the first or last row.
A drawing is good for what something looked like; a tally/table is good for how many — match the record to what you need to know.
activities.rationale: Reading a tally/table to answer a question and choosing an appropriate record type consolidate the read-back half of the skill, and can be used during teaching as well as to check understanding. This format exercises reading-back but does not require capture-in-the-moment, so it complements rather than replaces the live activity.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Working Scientifically requires gathering and recording data to help in answering questions.
learnerActions: Look at a completed tally or table and answer questions from it: 'which was seen most?', 'how many altogether?', 'which day had no rain?'
Given a set of results to collect (e.g. counts of three kinds of leaf), choose which simple record would suit it — a tally chart, a two-column count table, or a labelled drawing — and say why.
Match given data to the best simple record type.
activities.intendedInsight: A record only works if it can be read back to answer the question, and different simple records suit different kinds of information.

activities.title: Parts of a tally chart (reference scaffold)
feedback: Notice the fifth stroke crosses the other four to make a gate — this lets you count in fives.
Every row has a label so you always know which count belongs to which thing.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled example gives the child a model of what a well-structured record looks like. This is a support only: a reference image shows the structure but does not require the child to perform the active capture, so it should accompany, not substitute for, the live recording task.
learnerActions: Explore a labelled example tally chart and table: tap to reveal what each part is for — the heading row, one line per category, the gated group of five, the total.
Use this as a reference while setting up your own record in the capture activity.
activities.intendedInsight: A readable record has clear headings, one category per row, and tallies grouped in fives so they can be counted quickly.

constraints: Checkpoint is Tier A (concrete/observational): the bar is recording observations in a simple table or tally, using a labelled drawing, and saying how the record helps answer the question. Choosing between graph types comes later.
Builds on performing simple tests as a prerequisite and feeds forward to presenting data in charts/keys and analysing design tests.
Decide headings and categories BEFORE collecting so the table is ready to fill; avoid changing headings mid-collection, because the counts may no longer match up and become hard to total and compare.
Always close the loop: after recording, return to the question and ask what the record tells us.

The read-back/matching practice checks reading a record but does not elicit capture-in-the-moment; the reference image shows structure but does not require the child to construct a record. Both are scaffolds around the live capture task, not replacements for it.

Live on-screen scenes are one medium; equivalent real-world collection (tallying minibeasts, logging daily weather, rolling toy cars and recording distances) meets the same objective and should be used where practical.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS Appendix F source (SEP 4/SEP 8, K-2) was marked verified:false in the source row; treat that citation's confirmation status as unverified even though the claim supports the recording principle.

The diagnostic 'which car rolls furthest' task in the source assessment uses distance, which involves measurement/comparison; for the youngest learners a count-based scene (how many of each minibeast, which day was rainiest) may be a gentler entry to recording. Both are retained as context; neither is asserted as superior.

The source rated conversation and 3D artefacts as 'poor'/'no spatial dimension' and framed a static image as unable to 'require' active capture. These are presented here as narrowly scoped affordance notes (a reference image supports but does not require construction), not as universal claims that other media cannot teach recording.

probeDeeper: How does your record show which result belongs to which car?
Why write it down as you go instead of at the end?
Looking at your record, which car won? How can you tell?
If you'd just remembered the results, could you be sure? What might go wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: The child creates a simple organised record — a table or chart pairing each car with its distance (or a labelled tally/drawing) — records each result as they go, and can read from it to answer which car rolled furthest. The record is organised enough that the results can be compared.

errorPatterns.pattern: Disorganised or unlabelled record: writes numbers with no indication of which car they belong to.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each result with its car — a row or column per car so the record is readable later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The record is ambiguous — results can't be matched to cars afterwards.

errorPatterns.pattern: Relies on memory: does all the rolls first, then tries to remember the results to write down.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Record each result as it happens, so nothing is forgotten or mixed up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No recording happens during the activity itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Record not linked to the question: makes marks but can't use them to say which car won.
errorPatterns.nextMove: 'Look at your record — which car has the biggest number?' Tie the record back to the question.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child can't read an answer off their own record.

responseLevels.gap: Records nothing until the end, or writes marks with no labels that can't be interpreted afterwards.
responseLevels.full: Sets up a simple organised record (table, tally, or labelled drawing) pairing each item with its result, records as the activity happens, and reads the answer to the question directly off the record.
responseLevels.partial: Records results in a mostly organised way but needs prompting to label clearly or to link the record back to the question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We want to find out which of these three toy cars rolls the furthest. You'll roll each car and need to keep a record so we don't forget the results. Set up a way to write down what happens, then do the rolls and record them. Afterwards, tell me how your record helps answer which car won. I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who records systematically (a structure pairing each car with its result) from one who writes numbers with no labels, records nothing until the end (relying on memory), or makes marks they can't later interpret. The tell is whether the record can actually be used to answer the question.
